title: 22. Interview: CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)
summary: Interview Q&A for CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is CSRF and how does it differ from XSS?
**Answer:** CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) is an attack where a malicious site tricks the victim's browser into making an authenticated request to a target site where the victim is already logged in — the attacker rides the victim's existing session but never sees the credentials. XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is an attack where the attacker injects malicious JavaScript into a page viewed by other users — the script runs in the victim's browser with the victim's privileges and can read cookies, make authenticated requests, and exfiltrate data. The key difference: CSRF abuses the browser's automatic cookie attachment, while XSS abuses the same-origin policy's trust of JavaScript that runs within the page's origin. CSRF is "the browser does what the attacker wants as the victim"; XSS is "the attacker's code runs as the victim." Mitigations differ: CSRF is stopped with tokens, SameSite cookies, and Origin checks; XSS is stopped with output encoding, CSP, and HttpOnly cookies. XSS is strictly more powerful — an XSS vulnerability can bypass CSRF protections by reading the CSRF token from the page.

**Visual:**
```
CSRF:  evil.com -> [forces POST] -> bank.com (cookie auto-sent)
       attacker never sees cookie, just rides session

XSS:   evil script runs inside bank.com's page
       script reads cookie, reads CSRF token, exfiltrates data
       attacker effectively has full victim session
```

### Q2. How does a CSRF token work, and what are the synchronizer vs double-submit patterns?
**Answer:** A CSRF token is a random, unguessable value that the server generates per session (or per request) and embeds in every state-changing form as a hidden field or in a response header. On each POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE, the server validates that the submitted token matches what was issued; if not, the request is rejected. The security relies on the same-origin policy: an attacker's site cannot read the token from a `GET` to the target site (the response is cross-origin and blocked), so they cannot include it in their forged POST. The **synchronizer token pattern** stores the token server-side in the user's session and compares the submitted value — simple and secure, but requires session storage and a lookup per request. The **double-submit cookie pattern** is stateless: the server sets a cookie containing the token AND requires the same token in a request header; the server compares the two values without storing anything. The attacker cannot forge both because they cannot write cookies to the target's domain. The double-submit pattern is preferred for stateless or distributed backends; it can be hardened by HMAC-binding the cookie value to the session ID so an attacker cannot substitute their own token-cookie pair.

**Visual:**
```
SYNCHRONIZER:
  server: store token in session["csrf"]
  form:   <input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="...">
  POST:   compare form.csrf == session["csrf"]   (server-side lookup)

DOUBLE-SUBMIT:
  server: Set-Cookie: csrf=xyz; SameSite=Lax
  form/header: X-CSRF-Token: xyz
  POST:   compare cookie.csrf == header.csrf   (no server storage)
  hardened: cookie = HMAC(session_id, token) + token
```

### Q3. What are SameSite cookies and how do they mitigate CSRF?
**Answer:** SameSite is a cookie attribute (defined in RFC 6265bis) that controls whether a cookie is sent on cross-site requests. `SameSite=Strict` means the cookie is sent only when the request originates from the same site as the cookie's domain — no cross-site navigations, no cross-site POSTs. This fully defeats CSRF, but it breaks some UX patterns: clicking a link in an email to your bank's dashboard will appear logged-out (the cookie is not sent on the top-level navigation from a different site). `SameSite=Lax` is a compromise: the cookie is sent on top-level navigations (link clicks, form GETs) but not on cross-site POSTs, background requests, or iframes — so the classic CSRF POST attack is blocked while the email-link UX works. `SameSite=None; Secure` allows cross-site sending but requires HTTPS (and re-enables CSRF, so it must be paired with tokens). Chrome's default since 2020 is `Lax` for cookies without an explicit attribute, which eliminated a huge class of CSRF attacks across the web overnight. Best practice: session cookies should be `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict` where UX allows) plus `Secure` and `HttpOnly`.

**Visual:**
```
SameSite=Strict:  cookie sent only on same-site requests
  bank.com link from bank.com page  -> cookie sent
  bank.com link from email/gmail    -> cookie NOT sent (logged out)
  cross-site POST (CSRF)            -> cookie NOT sent (attack blocked)

SameSite=Lax:     cookie sent on top-level GET nav, not on POST/iframe
  bank.com link from email          -> cookie sent (UX works)
  cross-site POST (CSRF)            -> cookie NOT sent (attack blocked)
  cross-site background GET         -> cookie NOT sent

SameSite=None;Secure: cookie always sent (CSRF surface restored)
  -> must pair with CSRF tokens + Origin check
```

### Q4. Why does checking the Origin or Referer header help, and what are the caveats?
**Answer:** The `Origin` header (sent on CORS-relevant requests: POSTs, cross-origin requests, etc.) and `Referer` header (sent on most navigations) tell the server which site initiated the request. For a state-changing request, the server can compare the `Origin` against its own expected origin and reject if it doesn't match — a CSRF attack coming from `evil.com` will have `Origin: https://evil.com`, not `https://bank.com`, so it is rejected. The `Origin` header is preferred because it is sent only on cross-origin and state-changing requests (less privacy leaky than `Referer`, which leaks the full URL of the originating page) and cannot be spoofed by JavaScript in modern browsers (the `Origin` header is set by the browser, not the page). The caveats: `Origin` may be missing on some same-origin requests (then the server should accept or fall back to `Referer`), older browsers may not send it (use `Referer` as a fallback), and `Referer` can be suppressed by `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` (then fall back to token validation). Origin checking is a defense-in-depth layer, not a complete defense — pair it with tokens and SameSite cookies.

**Visual:**
```
legit request from bank.com:
  Origin: https://bank.com        -> matches expected, accept

CSRF from evil.com:
  Origin: https://evil.com        -> mismatch, REJECT

same-origin request (older browser, no Origin):
  Referer: https://bank.com/dashboard  -> matches, accept
  (fallback chain: Origin first, then Referer, then token)

privacy: Origin leaks only scheme+host+port
         Referer leaks full URL (path, query) -> prefer Origin
```

### Q5. Why does requiring a custom header (like X-Requested-With) mitigate CSRF?
**Answer:** A custom request header like `X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest` or `X-CSRF-Token` provides CSRF protection because of how CORS works: a cross-origin request that uses a "non-simple" header (any header other than `Accept`, `Accept-Language`, `Content-Language`, `Content-Type` of `text/plain`/`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`/`multipart/form-data`) triggers a CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) request, and the browser will not send the actual request unless the preflight response explicitly allows that header via `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. An attacker's site cannot set a custom header on a cross-origin request without the target's CORS permission — so if the server requires a custom header for state-changing requests, a CSRF attack (which has no CORS preflight permission) cannot include it, and the request is rejected. This is why Rails' `protect_from_forgery` accepts the `X-CSRF-Token` header as an alternative to the form field for AJAX calls. The caveat: this only protects against CSRF — it does not replace the token, because a CORS misconfiguration that allows `*` for headers and origins would re-enable the attack. Layer the defenses.

**Visual:**
```
attacker's form submission (simple request, no preflight):
  POST /transfer HTTP/1.1
  Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
  Cookie: session=abc
  body: to=attacker&amt=1000
  -> no custom header -> server REJECTS (requirement: X-CSRF-Token)

legit AJAX from same-origin SPA:
  POST /transfer HTTP/1.1
  X-CSRF-Token: <token>      <-- custom header
  Content-Type: application/json
  Cookie: session=abc
  -> header present -> server accepts

cross-origin AJAX (would need CORS preflight):
  browser sends OPTIONS first, server must allow X-CSRF-Token header
  attacker has no CORS permission -> preflight fails -> request blocked
```

### Q6. Are bearer-token APIs (Authorization: Bearer) vulnerable to CSRF?
**Answer:** APIs that authenticate via the `Authorization: Bearer <token>` header (where the application explicitly attaches the token, not the browser) are immune to CSRF by construction. The browser does not automatically attach `Authorization` headers — the application code does — so a cross-site request forged by `evil.com` will not include the bearer token, and the API rejects the request. CSRF specifically exploits cookies (and HTTP Basic auth, and client TLS certificates) because the browser auto-attaches them. The trade-off is where you store the bearer token: in `localStorage` (immune to CSRF, but vulnerable to XSS theft — any injected script can read `localStorage`), or in an `HttpOnly` cookie (immune to XSS theft, but vulnerable to CSRF — must pair with tokens and SameSite). The safest pattern for web apps is to keep the auth token in an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` cookie and use CSRF tokens; for mobile apps and SPAs with BFF (Backend-For-Frontend), use bearer tokens stored in memory (not localStorage) with refresh via an HttpOnly cookie. Mobile apps use bearer tokens in secure storage and are immune to CSRF because they don't have the browser's automatic cookie behavior.

**Visual:**
```
cookie-based auth (web app):
  browser auto-attaches Cookie on EVERY request to the origin
  -> CSRF attack works (browser sends cookie on attacker's forged POST)
  -> MUST use CSRF token + SameSite + Origin check

bearer-token auth (API/mobile):
  app explicitly sets Authorization: Bearer <token>
  browser does NOT auto-attach
  -> CSRF attack fails (attacker's POST has no Authorization header)
  -> but vulnerable to XSS if token is in localStorage

BFF / HttpOnly cookie + in-memory access token:
  refresh token in HttpOnly cookie (CSRF-protected)
  access token in JS memory (XSS can't read cookie, expires fast)
```

### Q7. How would you design CSRF protection for a single-page app (SPA) with a stateless JWT backend?
**Answer:** For an SPA with a stateless JWT backend, the recommended pattern is the BFF (Backend-For-Frontend) model: the SPA never handles tokens directly. The BFF (a small server-side component, often running on the same origin as the SPA) handles login, stores the refresh token in an `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Lax`, `Secure` cookie, and issues short-lived access tokens to the SPA via a same-origin endpoint that returns the token in the response body (not a cookie). The SPA holds the access token in memory (not localStorage) and uses it as a bearer token for API calls — immune to CSRF because the browser doesn't auto-attach it. When the access token expires, the SPA calls the BFF's refresh endpoint, which uses the HttpOnly cookie to authenticate — this refresh call IS vulnerable to CSRF, so the BFF must require a CSRF token (sync or double-submit) on the refresh endpoint. Alternatively, if the JWT itself is stored in an HttpOnly cookie, then ALL API calls are CSRF-vulnerable and must use CSRF tokens on every state-changing endpoint — pair with SameSite=Lax and Origin checking. The cleanest design: BFF with HttpOnly refresh cookie + in-memory access token + CSRF token on the refresh endpoint, and the SPA talks to the API via bearer tokens (no CSRF on API calls).

**Visual:**
```
SPA (browser)              BFF (same origin)         API (any origin)
   |                             |                          |
   | 1. POST /login (creds) ---->|                          |
   |<-- Set-Cookie: refresh -----|                          |
   |   (HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax,  |                          |
   |    Secure, CSRF-protected)  |                          |
   |                             |                          |
   | 2. POST /refresh            |                          |
   |    X-CSRF-Token: <token> -->|                          |
   |<-- access_token (in body) --|                          |
   |                             |                          |
   | 3. GET /api/data            |                          |
   |    Authorization: Bearer X->|------------------------->|
   |<-- data ---------------------|<-------------------------|
   |   (no CSRF needed: bearer    |                          |
   |    token not auto-attached)  |                          |
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. A security audit found that your web app's session cookie has no SameSite attribute and state-changing endpoints don't validate CSRF tokens. How do you remediate?
**Answer:** Immediate remediation: add `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict` if the UX allows) to all session and auth cookies, and ensure they are also `Secure` (HTTPS only) and `HttpOnly` (no JS access). Then enable CSRF token middleware in your framework (Django's `CsrfViewMiddleware`, Rails' `protect_from_forgery`, Express's `csurf` or `csrf-csrf`, Spring Security's CSRF) and verify that every form includes the token and every state-changing endpoint validates it. Add an `Origin` header check on all state-changing endpoints as defense-in-depth. Next, deploy to staging and run a CSRF test (use OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite's CSRF scanner, or manually craft a cross-site form) to verify the protection works. Then deploy to production behind a feature flag, monitor for false positives (legitimate users being blocked — usually caused by overly strict `SameSite=Strict` or an `Origin` check that rejects internal proxies that strip the header), and roll forward. Long-term: add CSRF protection to your CI test suite (assert that POSTs without tokens return 403), set a Content Security Policy that limits form-action destinations, and review all third-party integrations that might require `SameSite=None` cookies (handle those with explicit CSRF tokens and CORS restrictions).

**Visual:**
```
BEFORE (vulnerable):
  Set-Cookie: session=abc; HttpOnly
  POST /transfer -> server executes (no token check)

AFTER (remediated):
  Set-Cookie: session=abc; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
  POST /transfer -> server checks:
    1. CSRF token in form matches session (sync token)
    2. Origin header == https://app.example.com
    3. (AJAX) X-CSRF-Token header present
  -> all three pass -> execute
  -> any fail -> 403 Forbidden
```

### Q2. Your team is building a mobile app and a web app against the same API. The web app uses cookie-based auth; the mobile app uses bearer tokens. Do you need CSRF protection on the API?
**Answer:** The API needs CSRF protection only for endpoints that accept cookie-based authentication — i.e., the web app's requests. The mobile app's requests use bearer tokens in the `Authorization` header, which the browser (or the mobile HTTP client) does not auto-attach, so they are immune to CSRF. The cleanest design is to require a CSRF token (or custom header) on all state-changing endpoints, but document that the mobile app satisfies this via the bearer token's `Authorization` header (which is, itself, a custom header requiring CORS preflight on cross-origin requests — but mobile apps don't have a CORS concept). If the API accepts both auth methods, the middleware should be: "if the request is cookie-authenticated, require a valid CSRF token + Origin check; if it's bearer-token-authenticated, skip CSRF (the bearer token is the proof of intent)." This dual-mode is common in frameworks like Django REST Framework (which has `SessionAuthentication` requiring CSRF and `TokenAuthentication` not requiring it). The risk to avoid: if you skip CSRF on all endpoints because "the mobile app doesn't need it," the web app's cookie-authenticated requests become vulnerable. Always require CSRF for cookie-authenticated state changes, regardless of how many other clients also call the API.

**Visual:**
```
mobile app -> API:
  Authorization: Bearer <jwt>
  -> bearer token, no auto-attach, CSRF-immune
  -> middleware: skip CSRF check, validate JWT

web app -> API:
  Cookie: session=abc
  X-CSRF-Token: <token>
  Origin: https://app.example.com
  -> cookie-based, CSRF-vulnerable without protection
  -> middleware: require X-CSRF-Token, validate against session,
     check Origin

middleware logic:
  if request has Authorization header -> bearer auth -> skip CSRF
  elif request has session cookie -> cookie auth -> require CSRF
  else -> 401 unauthenticated
```

### Q3. You deploy SameSite=Strict cookies to fix CSRF, and users start reporting they can't log in from email links. What happened and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** `SameSite=Strict` cookies are not sent when the request originates from a different site, even on top-level GET navigations. So when a user clicks a link in an email (from `mail.google.com` or `outlook.com`) to your app (`app.example.com`), the browser loads the page but does not send the session cookie — the user appears logged out. The same problem occurs with SSO redirects: when the IdP redirects back to your SP, the SP's session cookie is not sent, so the user can't complete the SSO flow. The fix is to use `SameSite=Lax` instead of `Strict`: `Lax` sends the cookie on top-level GET navigations from any site, so email links and SSO redirects work, but it still blocks cross-site POSTs (the actual CSRF attack vector). If you need `Strict` for higher security on specific cookies (e.g., admin session), use a two-minute `Lax` cookie to bridge the navigation and then upgrade to `Strict` after a same-origin request confirms the user is interacting with the app. Or: use a "warm-up" endpoint that the email link hits first (same-origin), which sets a `Lax` cookie that then allows the subsequent authenticated navigation. The pragmatic answer is `SameSite=Lax` for the common case, paired with CSRF tokens and Origin checks — this matches what Google, GitHub, and most large sites do.

**Visual:**
```
SameSite=Strict (too strict):
  email link -> app.example.com/dashboard
  browser: GET, top-level nav from mail.google.com
  -> cookie NOT sent (Strict blocks cross-site nav)
  -> user sees "logged out" page  (bug!)

SameSite=Lax (correct default):
  email link -> app.example.com/dashboard
  browser: GET, top-level nav
  -> cookie sent (Lax allows top-level GET nav)
  -> user sees dashboard (works)
  cross-site POST (CSRF) -> cookie NOT sent (Lax blocks POST)
  -> attack blocked

upgrade pattern (high security):
  initial: SameSite=Lax session cookie (2 min TTL)
  after first same-origin request: set SameSite=Strict (long TTL)
```

### Q4. Your SPA uses fetch to call the API with credentials: 'include' and the API uses cookie-based auth. After enabling SameSite=Lax, your POST requests fail. How do you debug?
**Answer:** The most likely cause is that the SPA's origin and the API's origin are different sites (e.g., SPA at `app.example.com` and API at `api.example.com` — these are same-site but might be treated differently if you have a public-suffix-list issue, or if they're on completely different domains like `app.com` and `api.com`). If they are different sites, `SameSite=Lax` blocks the cookie on cross-site POSTs, so the API sees no session and rejects. The fixes: (1) serve the SPA and API from the same site (e.g., `app.example.com` for SPA and `api.example.com` for API — both under `example.com` site, so cookies flow with `SameSite=Lax`); (2) if they must be different sites, use `SameSite=None; Secure` for the auth cookie (re-enables CSRF surface, so you MUST pair with CSRF tokens + Origin check); (3) switch to bearer tokens in the SPA's `Authorization` header (CSRF-immune, but you must store the token securely — prefer the BFF pattern with HttpOnly refresh cookie). Also verify CORS: with `credentials: 'include'`, the API must respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: <specific origin>` (not `*`) and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and the SPA's fetch must include `credentials: 'include'`. Debug steps: open DevTools → Network tab → click the failing request → check the Request Headers (is `Cookie` present?) and Response (status code 401/403?). If no cookie, it's SameSite; if cookie but 403, it's CORS or CSRF token.

**Visual:**
```
SPA at app.example.com -> API at api.example.com  (same site)
  cookie SameSite=Lax -> sent on cross-origin same-site POST  (works)

SPA at app.com -> API at api.com  (different sites)
  cookie SameSite=Lax -> NOT sent on cross-site POST  (fails)
  options:
    (a) SameSite=None; Secure + CSRF token + Origin check
    (b) move SPA and API under one site (recommended)
    (c) bearer token in Authorization header (no cookies)

CORS requirements for credentials: 'include':
  Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.com   (specific, not *)
  Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
  cookie attrs: Secure, SameSite=None (if cross-site)
```

### Q5. You discover that an internal admin tool has no CSRF protection and is reachable from the corporate network. What's your risk assessment and remediation plan?
**Answer:** Risk assessment: HIGH. Internal admin tools are high-value targets because they often have privileged actions (user impersonation, data export, configuration changes, financial approvals). An attacker can craft a CSRF payload and deliver it via a phishing email to an admin ("check this HR document") — when the admin clicks the link in their browser while logged into the admin tool, the forged POST executes with admin privileges. Even though the tool is "internal," if an admin's browser can reach it from the corporate network, the attack works — and remote workers on VPN, contractors, and compromised endpoints expand the surface. The attacker doesn't need to be on the corporate network; they just need the admin's browser to be. Remediation plan: (1) Immediate: add CSRF tokens to all state-changing endpoints, set `SameSite=Lax` (or `Strict`) on session cookies, validate `Origin` headers, and require a custom header (e.g., `X-Requested-With`) on all admin POSTs. (2) Short-term: enforce SSO + MFA for admin access (reduces credential theft, though doesn't stop CSRF itself), add network-level restrictions (admin tool only accessible from a bastion host or specific IP ranges), and add audit logging for all admin actions. (3) Long-term: move admin tools behind a zero-trust proxy (Cloudflare Access, Google BeyondCorp, AWS Verified Access) that requires device posture + identity verification on every request, and consider a separate admin browser profile or dedicated admin workstation. (4) Add an annual penetration test that includes CSRF specifically.

**Visual:**
```
ATTACK:
  admin (logged in to admin.corp) clicks phishing link
  -> evil.com page auto-POSTs to admin.corp/users/delete?id=42
  -> browser sends admin session cookie
  -> admin tool deletes user (no CSRF check)
  -> attacker achieved admin action without admin creds

REMEDIATION:
  admin.corp POST /users/delete:
    - require X-CSRF-Token (sync token, server-stored)
    - check Origin == https://admin.corp
    - session cookie: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict
    - require MFA re-auth for destructive actions
    - behind zero-trust proxy (Cloudflare Access)
    - audit log: who/what/when, alert on bulk deletes
```

### Q6. Your framework's CSRF middleware rejects legitimate requests from users behind corporate proxies. How do you handle it?
**Answer:** The likely cause is that the corporate proxy strips or rewrites the `Origin` or `Referer` header (some proxies do this for "privacy"), so the CSRF middleware sees a missing or unexpected Origin and rejects. The fix has several options: (1) Treat a missing `Origin` header as a soft check — if `Origin` is absent, fall back to `Referer` (also check it's the expected origin), and if both are absent, allow only if the request is a same-site request verified another way (e.g., the CSRF token is valid — the token is the primary defense, Origin is defense-in-depth). (2) For known corporate proxies, allowlist their source IP ranges or their rewritten Origin values in the middleware configuration (less ideal, but pragmatic). (3) Better: don't reject on Origin alone — always require the CSRF token (which the proxy cannot strip because it's in the request body or a custom header), and use Origin as a "block if present and wrong" check rather than "block if absent." The robust pattern: token is the primary defense (always required, validated per session); Origin/Referer is a secondary check that rejects if present and unexpected, but does not reject if absent (because some legitimate proxies strip them). Document this in your security policy and add test cases for both present-Origin and absent-Origin requests. Also, file a bug with the proxy vendor — stripping `Origin` is non-compliant with modern web standards and weakens the security posture of every site behind the proxy.

**Visual:**
```
normal request:
  Origin: https://app.example.com   -> matches, accept (token also valid)

corporate proxy strips Origin:
  (no Origin header)                -> don't reject on absence alone
  Referer: https://app.example.com/...  -> matches, accept
  CSRF token: <valid>               -> primary defense, accept

malicious request (CSRF):
  Origin: https://evil.com          -> mismatch, REJECT
  (token absent or invalid)         -> REJECT (primary defense)

policy:
  token: ALWAYS required, ALWAYS validated
  Origin: reject if present AND unexpected
          accept if absent (fall back to Referer)
  Referer: reject if present AND unexpected
           accept if absent (rare, log for monitoring)
```

### Q7. You're building a public form (like a contact-us form) that anyone can submit, including anonymous users. How do you protect it from CSRF and abuse?
**Answer:** Anonymous forms still need protection, but the threat model is different: there's no session to ride, so classic CSRF (which exploits an existing session) is not the concern — but cross-site form submission abuse is. An attacker could embed your form's action URL in a hidden form on their site and auto-submit spam or abuse payloads to your endpoint, making it look like your form is the source. Mitigations: (1) CSRF token even for anonymous users — issue a token tied to an anonymous session cookie (or a stateless HMAC-signed token) when the form is rendered, and validate on POST. The attacker's site can't read the token (SOP), so they can't forge submissions. (2) Rate limiting by IP and by fingerprint (User-Agent + IP hash) — Django's `django-ratelimit`, or a Redis-backed limiter. (3) Honeypot field — a hidden field named `website` or `url` that real users won't fill but bots will; reject submissions with it populated. (4) Time-based check — reject submissions that arrive less than 2 seconds after the form was rendered (bots submit instantly) or more than 1 hour later (the token was scraped). (5) CAPTCHA for repeat offenders — use Cloudflare Turnstile (privacy-preserving, no puzzle) or reCAPTCHA Enterprise, triggered after a few submissions from the same IP. (6) Content scanning — reject submissions with too many URLs, known spam patterns, or LLM-detected spam. (7) For high-volume abuse, require email verification before the submission is acted on (don't block the submit, but don't act until the email is verified). Layer these: token + rate limit + honeypot catches 99% of abuse; CAPTCHA catches the rest.

**Visual:**
```
anonymous form protection layers:
  1. CSRF token (anonymous session-bound, prevents cross-site forge)
  2. honeypot field (hidden "website" input, bots fill it, reject)
  3. rate limit per IP (e.g., 5 submissions/hour)
  4. timing check (reject if < 2s after render or > 1h after)
  5. content scan (URLs, spam patterns, LLM classifier)
  6. CAPTCHA after N suspicious submissions (Turnstile/reCAPTCHA)
  7. email verification before action (for high-trust workflows)

flow:
  GET /contact -> render form with token + honeypot + timestamp cookie
  POST /contact -> validate token, check honeypot empty, check timing,
                   check rate limit, scan content, accept or CAPTCHA
  if abuse pattern -> require CAPTCHA on subsequent submissions
  if persistent -> require email verification, throttle aggressively
```

quiz.explanation: synchronizer token pattern** stores the token server-side in the user's session and compares the submitted value — simple and secure, but requires session storage and a lookup per request. The double-submit cookie pattern is stateless: the server sets a cookie containing the token AND requires the same token in a request header; the server compares the two values without storing anything.

SameSite is a cookie attribute (defined in RFC 6265bis) that controls whether a cookie is sent on cross-site requests.
quiz.explanation: SameSite is a cookie attribute (defined in RFC 6265bis) that controls whether a cookie is sent on cross-site requests. SameSite=Strict means the cookie is sent only when the request originates from the same site as the cookie's domain — no cross-site navigations, no cross-site POSTs.
